prompt: Why block a dangerous site by its name at the resolver rather than by its address at a firewall?
hint: Which of the two moves more often?

choices.text: Because a firewall cannot block outbound traffic at all, only inbound
choices.why: Firewalls block outbound traffic every day; lesson 10 writes such rules.

choices.text: Addresses move and are shared; the name is the stable part
choices.why: Right. One name can answer with many addresses, and one address can carry a hundred sites.

choices.text: Because DNS is encrypted and firewalls cannot read it
choices.why: Ordinary DNS on port 53 is plain text; the encrypted kinds are this lesson's limits.

choices.text: Because a resolver is cheaper to buy than a firewall
choices.why: Price is not the argument; what each one can recognise is.

prompt: Before the lesson, desk's /etc/resolv.conf named 8.8.8.8. Where did that come from?

choices.text: From the firm's DHCP server, which hands it to every machine
choices.why: The lab has no DHCP server; the addresses are fixed.

choices.text: From dns, which announced itself as Google's resolver
choices.why: dns was not running a resolver yet, and resolvers do not announce themselves.

choices.text: Copied from the lab computer when the container booted
choices.why: Right. It is nobody's decision, which is the usual state of a small office.

prompt: What does `access-control: 192.168.60.0/24 allow` protect against?

choices.text: Machines on the segment asking for blocked names
choices.why: They are exactly the ones allowed; the policy zone handles blocked names.

choices.text: The resolver answering anybody outside the firm
choices.why: Right. An open resolver serves strangers and can be used against third parties.

choices.text: Forged answers arriving from the forwarder on trap, which the line rejects
choices.why: Validating answers is DNSSEC's job; this line is about who may ask.

choices.text: Two copies of unbound starting on the same port
choices.why: The port is decided by interface lines, and a second copy would just fail to bind.

prompt: The lesson removes root-auto-trust-anchor-file.conf on dns. What would a real firm's resolver keep by leaving it in place?
hint: It needs the internet to work.

choices.text: Its log of every question, which that file switches on
choices.why: The log comes from log-queries in the firm's own file.

choices.text: The policy zones, which need the root to be trusted before they load
choices.why: The policy zones loaded here with the file removed.

choices.text: DNSSEC validation, which checks that each answer is genuine
choices.why: Right. With internet access it fetches the root key and checks signatures.

choices.text: Access for clients outside 192.168.60.0/24
choices.why: That is access-control, and widening it would be a mistake.

prompt: desk asks dns for www.ubuntu.com and gets SERVFAIL. What does that status mean?

choices.text: The resolver tried and could not get any answer for that name
choices.why: Right. trap, playing the internet, does not answer for that name.

choices.text: The name was found on the blocklist and refused on purpose
choices.why: The list answers NXDOMAIN or an address, and no list existed yet.

choices.text: The name exists, but has no address of the type asked for
choices.why: That is NOERROR with an empty answer, called NODATA.

choices.text: desk is not allowed to use this resolver
choices.why: A refused client gets REFUSED, and desk's own name resolved a second earlier.

prompt: Why does the lesson call the resolver's query log the cheapest telemetry a small firm can have?

choices.text: Because it records the contents of every web page visited
choices.why: It records names asked for, not what was fetched.

choices.text: Because DNS logs are smaller than any other kind of log there is
choices.why: Size is not the point, and a busy resolver writes a lot.

choices.text: It needs no agent on any machine, because every machine already asks it
choices.why: Right. Every machine already asks it, so every machine is covered.

choices.text: Because the law requires firms to keep it, so it is already paid for
choices.why: No such obligation was mentioned, and it would not make it cheap.

prompt: Match each line of a policy zone with what desk receives.
hint: Look at the action, not the name.

prompt: Which names does the entry `*.cobranca-urgente.example.org` match?

choices.text: Only the name cobranca-urgente.example.org itself
choices.why: The asterisk is for the names below it.

choices.text: Every name in example.org, whatever comes before it
choices.why: The wildcard sits under cobranca-urgente, not under example.org.

choices.text: Every name below cobranca-urgente.example.org, at any depth
choices.why: Right, pagamento.cobranca-urgente.example.org among them.

choices.text: Names that contain cobranca anywhere in them
choices.why: DNS wildcards match whole labels on the left, not substrings.

prompt: The log shows `rpz: applied [feed] ... 192.168.60.20`. Besides the block itself, what has the firm gained?

choices.text: A finding: desk tried to reach a listed domain
choices.why: Right. Somebody can look at desk without anybody having reported anything.

choices.text: Proof that desk is infected and has to be rebuilt today
choices.why: A lookup can come from a preview or a scanner; it starts an investigation, it does not end one.

choices.text: The name of the person who was logged in to desk at the time
choices.why: The resolver sees an address, not a person.

choices.text: A copy of the page that desk was trying to open
choices.why: Nothing was fetched; the name never resolved.

prompt: Why does the lesson answer one listed domain with an address instead of NXDOMAIN?

choices.text: Because NXDOMAIN is cached for longer and slows the network down
choices.why: Caching is not the reason; what happens next is.

choices.text: So the program connects somewhere that records what it wanted
choices.why: Right. The sinkhole saw the path /boleto.pdf, which the lookup alone could not show.

choices.text: Because an address is the only answer browsers accept
choices.why: Browsers handle NXDOMAIN all the time; it is a missing site.

choices.text: To send the program back to its real destination by another route
choices.why: The real site is never reached; that is the point.

prompt: Every blocked name in a wildcard family points at the same sinkhole address. How did the sinkhole's log still know which name desk wanted?
hint: What does a browser send along with the path?

choices.text: It asked the resolver which name had just been sinkholed
choices.why: The sinkhole program asks nobody; it reads the request.

choices.text: From the Host header of the HTTP request
choices.why: Right. HTTP carries the name the client meant in every request.

choices.text: From the reverse lookup of desk's address
choices.why: That gives desk's name, not the site's.

choices.text: It cannot: the log only shows the address desk connected from, never the name
choices.why: The log line has the name in it: pagamento.cobranca-urgente.example.org.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson's sinkhole NOT do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Remove whatever made desk go there
choices.why: It cleans nothing; the machine is examined separately.

choices.text: Show a person a page saying the site is blocked
choices.why: It does: one line, instead of an error.

choices.text: Answer a program that connects with TLS on port 443
choices.why: It speaks plain HTTP on port 80 only.

choices.text: Record the address of the machine that connected
choices.why: It does: 192.168.60.20 is in its log.

prompt: How does an RPZ feed kept by another organisation usually reach a resolver?

choices.text: Somebody downloads it each morning and pastes it into the configuration
choices.why: That is a hosts-style list at best; an RPZ feed refreshes itself.

choices.text: By zone transfer from their server
choices.why: Right: AXFR or IXFR, with primary: lines in Unbound.

choices.text: Through an agent installed on every workstation of the firm
choices.why: Agents are a vendor service's shape; RPZ lives in the resolver.

choices.text: Inside the operating system's updates
choices.why: Operating system updates carry no blocklists.

prompt: A colleague puts the allowlist's rpz: block after the feed's. jatoba.contabil-nuvem.example.net is on both. What happens?
hint: Unbound stops at the first zone that matches.

choices.text: The allowlist wins, because passthru is always stronger than a block
choices.why: No action outranks another; the order of the zones decides.

choices.text: unbound-checkconf refuses the file because the zones overlap
choices.why: Overlapping zones are allowed; that is how allowlists work at all.

choices.text: The feed matches first, and the name stays blocked
choices.why: Right. That is why the allowlist goes first.

choices.text: The two actions are combined, and desk gets both answers
choices.why: A question gets one answer.

prompt: What should come with every allowlist entry, according to the lesson?

choices.text: A copy of the feed entry it overrides, so both can be compared
choices.why: Useful context, and not what makes it safe to keep.

choices.text: The approval of the feed's publisher
choices.why: The publisher is not asked; the decision is the firm's.

choices.text: A reason, an owner and a date to review it
choices.why: Right. The domain allowed today may be taken over next year.

choices.text: A second entry in the feed itself, to keep the two lists in step
choices.why: The feed is somebody else's; you do not edit it.

prompt: Before a new broad feed starts blocking, the lesson suggests a week of rpz-action-override: disabled. What does that week give you?

choices.text: A log of what it would have broken, with nothing blocked yet
choices.why: Right. The zone is read and logged but not applied.

choices.text: A faster resolver, because the feed is cached in advance
choices.why: Speed is not what the setting is for.

choices.text: Time for the feed's publisher to remove its false positives
choices.why: They do not know about your false positives unless you tell them.

choices.text: A blocked list that users can test without any risk to their work
choices.why: Nothing is blocked during that week.

prompt: `dig @192.168.60.66 boletos-jatoba.example.net` from desk returned the real address. Why?

choices.text: The policy zone had expired after 300 seconds
choices.why: 300 is the lifetime of answers, not of the zone; dns still blocked it.

choices.text: desk asked another resolver, which has no list
choices.why: Right. The control only covers questions that reach dns.

choices.text: dig ignores policy zones when an address is given
choices.why: dig does not know about policy zones; the resolver applies them.

choices.text: The allowlist covered that name too
choices.why: The allowlist names only jatoba.contabil-nuvem.example.net.

prompt: Why is the rule against other resolvers put on the switch rather than on desk?

choices.text: Because nftables does not run on workstations
choices.why: It runs on desk as well as anywhere; lesson 5 uses it on web.

choices.text: Because a rule on desk would also block questions to dns
choices.why: The same exception for dns could be written there.

choices.text: One rule covers every machine, and none of them can undo it
choices.why: Right. A program on desk with root could remove a rule on desk.

choices.text: Because the switch is the only machine that can see port 53
choices.why: Every machine sees its own traffic on port 53.

prompt: Which of these walk past the switch rule on port 53? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A browser using DNS over HTTPS
choices.why: Its questions travel inside HTTPS on port 443.

choices.text: A program with an address written into it
choices.why: It asks no resolver at all.

choices.text: A laptop configured to ask 8.8.8.8
choices.why: That is exactly what the rule stops.

choices.text: dig @192.168.60.66 run on desk
choices.why: The transcript shows it timing out.

prompt: Put in order what happens when desk opens a link to a sinkholed name.
items: desk asks dns for the name
the policy zone matches and dns answers 192.168.60.53
desk connects to 192.168.60.53 and asks for the file
the sinkhole logs the address, the name and the path

prompt: Put the firm's resolver configuration in the order the lesson needs it written.
hint: Unbound reads policy zones in order.
items: server: who may ask, and the firm's own names

prompt: Which port does DNS over TLS use, the one that can be blocked like 53?
In a policy zone, `name CNAME rpz-___.` tells the resolver to answer that name truthfully.
A manager reads this lesson and says the firm no longer needs outbound firewall rules. What is the best reply?

choices.text: Agreed, as long as the feed is refreshed every hour
choices.why: A fresher list does nothing for programs that never ask.

choices.text: Agreed, because the switch rule already stops every other resolver
choices.why: It stops port 53, not DoH or a hard-coded address.

choices.text: No: DNS covers programs that ask; outbound rules cover the rest
choices.why: Right. It is one cheap, wide layer, not the only one.

choices.text: No: DNS blocking is too easy to bypass to be worth running
choices.why: It covers every ordinary program on every machine and gives the best log; that is worth a lot.
